"Northern Territory police failed to act on a string of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles before the death of a vulnerable 23-year-old man last year, a coroner has found.

NT coroner Greg Cavanagh has criticised police for failing to act on an internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged vehicles in 2013, following an earlier death in custody.

In the three years between the two deaths, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in caged vehicles.

“In six cases the persons were not detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious,” Cavanagh found. “It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.”

On 16 September last year, two officers were making their way through Darwin, on their way to investigate a noise complaint, when they came across the scene of a serious crash.

A Toyota Hilux had smashed into a palm tree on the corner of the Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, not far from Darwin airport.

Hiding behind some vegetation was Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23. Walkinshaw was unharmed but held his passenger in his arms. The young woman, whom he had met earlier at a bar, was in and out of consciousness, having suffered an injury to her back.

Walkinshaw was well over the limit, returning a reading of 0.149.

The coroner found Walkinshaw was distressed, intoxicated and afraid when police took him into custody. He repeatedly asked about the woman’s condition and became increasingly agitated when officers were unable to give him clear answers.

Cavanagh said that, while police were entitled to arrest Walkinshaw over the crash and suspected drink-driving offences, they failed to properly assess his vulnerability before placing him in the rear cage of the van.

The inquest heard the vehicle used to transport him had no camera monitoring system, despite years of warnings about the risk of detainees harming themselves while hidden from view.

Officers checked on Walkinshaw only intermittently during the journey and after arriving at the watch house. By the time they realised he was in serious distress, critical minutes had passed.

Paramedics were called and efforts were made to revive him, but Walkinshaw was later pronounced dead.

Cavanagh said the death was preventable and represented a systemic failure rather than a single lapse by individual officers.

He said the 2013 recommendation for CCTV in police vans had been allowed to drift through bureaucracy, despite repeated evidence that detainees in the caged compartments were at significant risk.

“The knowledge was there,” the coroner said. “The warning signs were there. The means of reducing the risk were identified. What was lacking was urgency.”

The coroner recommended that all Northern Territory police vehicles used to transport detainees be fitted with CCTV and audio monitoring, that officers receive improved training in identifying mental distress and intoxication-related vulnerability, and that detainees be continuously monitored where there is any risk of self-harm.

Walkinshaw’s family, who attended parts of the inquest, said outside court that they welcomed the findings but remained devastated that action had not been taken earlier.

They described him as a young man who had struggled at times but was loved deeply by his relatives and friends.

“No family should have to hear that their son died because warnings were ignored,” a family member said.

Northern Territory police said they accepted the coroner’s findings and had begun reviewing transport procedures. A spokesperson said the force was working to install monitoring equipment across its fleet and improve safety protocols for detainees.

But Cavanagh said promises of reform would not be enough unless they were matched by immediate action.

“This death occurred in circumstances that were foreseeable,” he said. “The community is entitled to expect that when a person is taken into police custody, their life will be protected.”"
